item.title: Vatican confirms Pope Leo's Latin America trip after post-surgery checkup
item.description:
Vatican confirms Pope Leo's Latin America trip after post-surgery checkup
Pope Leo XIV will proceed with his planned trip to Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru.ByThe Associated PressOctober 26, 2026, 12:53 PM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
VATICAN CITY -- VATICAN CITY (AP) — Pope Leo XIV will proceed with his planned Nov. 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, after doctors determined there are no medical reasons preventing him from traveling three weeks after lung cancer surgery, the Vatican confirmed Monday.
The Vatican press office said the pope’s recovery continues to progress in line with favorable assessments from his medical team. It also confirmed the pope is keeping the already ambitious trip program with no announced changes.
Surgeons on Oct. 13 removed a lobe where the nodule later diagnosed as malignant was located, in the first major health event of Leo's 17-month pontificate. The surgery confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer.
Since returning to the Vatican, Leo has gradually resumed his activities while adjusting his schedule to prioritize recovery and periods of rest, the statement said.
The pope’s physician, Luigi Carbone, said there's no medical reason preventing Leo's trip to South America, which involves a dozen flights and two helicopter rides to high altitudes.

item.title: In Serbia and Hungary, groundswells of youthful energy topple entrenched governments
item.description:
In Serbia and Hungary, groundswells of youthful energy topple entrenched governments
Serbia has seen a dramatic shift after President Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat to student-backed candidatesByJOVANA GEC Associated Press and JUSTIN SPIKE Associated PressOctober 26, 2026, 11:32 AM
BELGRADE, Serbia -- For over a year, residents of Serbia's capital were blocked from entering one of the city's most prominent parks, nestled between Parliament and the offices of the powerful right-wing leader, Aleksandar Vucic.
The reason: the park in Belgrade had been cordoned off and occupied by throngs of Vucic's most ardent — and violent — supporters, an effective enforcer squad for the authoritarian leader tasked with intimidating and sometimes assaulting members of a growing anti-government student movement.
But after Vucic stunned the Balkan country Sunday evening by conceding defeat in an election against student-backed candidates, ecstatic young revelers filled the streets of Belgrade and ripped down the cordons around the encampment known as Caciland. Before long, the barricades lay tossed aside and the tents within went up in smoke, along with Vucic's power.
The seismic shift came after two years of relentless organizing and sustained protests by the student movement, which accused the Kremlin-backed Vucic of increasing authoritarianism, connections to organized crime and runaway corruption.
It also echoed other bottom-up, youth-led protest movements that have recently challenged what they see as entrenched, unresponsive power structures in Europe and beyond. Close to home, in neighboring Hungary, they succeeded in ousting another entrenched leader.

item.title: A cartoonist takes Japan’s new imperial succession law to court over male-only heirs
item.description:
A cartoonist takes Japan’s new imperial succession law to court over male-only heirs
A popular Japanese cartoonist has sued the government over a revised imperial succession lawByMARI YAMAGUCHI Associated PressOctober 26, 2026, 10:39 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
TOKYO -- A popular Japanese cartoonist who has written books on history and monarchy has sued the government over a revised imperial succession law allowing royals to adopt male relatives from former branch families to father future heirs.
The revised law took effect Saturday despite criticism over the male-only succession rules in Japan's 1,500-year-old monarchy. Next in line after Emperor Naruhito is his younger brother Akishino, followed by the emperor's 20-year-old nephew, Prince Hisahito. There are no other eligible heirs in his generation.
The revised law allows adoption of unmarried male descendants, aged 15 or older, of distant imperial relatives, but only through an unbroken male line, into a branch of the royal family. They would not be able to inherit the throne themselves, but their heirs would be eligible.
Four of the 11 former branch families who renounced their royal status in 1947 remain. Officials say they are at least 36 generations removed from Naruhito after splitting from a common male-line ancestor 600 years ago. Critics say they are too distant to be considered relatives.
In his lawsuit, Yoshinori Kobayashi says the adoption of former royals, who are commoners, discriminates against other commoners in violation of Article 14 of the constitution, which guarantees equality regardless of “race, creed, sex, social status or family origin.”
"The adoption would introduce a new class system of ‘former imperial branch family’ in Japan. ... It's a serious problem," Kobayashi told reporters after filing the lawsuit with the Tokyo District Court, a first legal step against the revised law. No trial date has been set.

item.title: Lula secures victory in Brazil, but faces challenge as Bolsonaro contests victory
item.description:
Lula secures victory in Brazil, but faces challenge as Bolsonaro contests victory
Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has won reelection in Brazil's presidential runoffByANNA-CATHERINE BRIGIDA Associated Press and MAURICIO SAVARESE Associated PressOctober 26, 2026, 9:53 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
BRASILIA -- President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva 's comeback to win Brazil’s presidential runoff Sunday is already facing its first hurdle as his competitor, Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, challenges the results, setting the stage for a possible showdown between the country’s two polarizing political forces.
Lula, who convinced an extra 10.4 million voters to support him in the runoff, is expected to take office on Jan. 5, 2027, for his fourth non-consecutive term. He will serve as a counterweight in a region where leaders are shifting to the right and aligning with U.S. President Donald Trump. Bolsonaro, son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, promised to cozy up to the Trump administration.
At a news conference Sunday, Bolsonaro said he planned to request an annulment of the election following a chaotic extension of voting at the request of both candidates. However, it's unclear what legal avenue he would have to do that. His father also contested his loss to Lula four years ago and now serves a 27-year prison sentence for a coup attempt.
Early signs from Brazil’s institutions and from leaders across the region, including conservative presidents who oppose Lula, suggest the results will be respected nationally and internationally. Trump has yet to weigh in.
Even with the vote extension, Lula’s win was decisive. The soon-to-be 81-year-old incumbent won more than 64 million votes compared to just under 60 million for Bolsonaro, a margin of nearly 4%.
President of Brazil’s electoral authority, Kassio Nunes, who was appointed to the Supreme Court by ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, was among those who recognized Lula’s victory Sunday.

item.title: Macron promises measures in response to French students' demands after weeks of unrest
item.description:
Macron promises measures in response to French students' demands after weeks of unrest
France will introduce “concrete measures” to address high school students’ demands for better resources and learning conditions after weeks of protests, school blockades and demonstrations, President Emmanuel Macron saidBySYLVIE CORBET Associated PressOctober 26, 2026, 9:47 AM
Share
PARIS -- French President Emmanuel Macron said the government would announce “concrete measures" on Monday to address school students’ demands for more resources and better learning conditions, after weeks of class boycotts, blockades and demonstrations that have grown into nationwide unrest.
“I have asked the government to address the legitimate demands at the root of this protest movement,” Macron said during a visit to the southern port city of Marseille, where protesters briefly stormed City Hall during rioting and looting on Oct. 17.
“The prime minister and government ministers will announce several major, concrete measures this afternoon,” Macron said.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu and other government officials were scheduled to meet with high school and university students later Monday.
Macron and his centrist government have faced criticism for failing to address students’ grievances since high school blockades began in mid-September. The protests have led to mass arrests and scrutiny of police riot-control weapons blamed for life-changing injuries suffered by some teenagers.
The Oct. 17 demonstrations against rising living costs and poor school conditions descended into violence, with groups setting fires, storming public buildings, looting shops and clashing with police in France’s worst unrest in years.

item.title: Swiss Ebola patient in Nigeria evacuated to Switzerland
item.description:
Swiss Ebola patient in Nigeria evacuated to Switzerland
A Swiss woman being treated for Ebola in Nigeria has been medically evacuated to Switzerland with her husbandByDYEPKAZAH SHIBAYAN Associated Press and MARK BANCHEREAU Associated PressOctober 26, 2026, 9:13 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
ABUJA, Nigeria -- A Swiss woman being treated for Ebola in Nigeria was medically evacuated to Switzerland with her husband Monday, officials said, as Nigerian authorities continued monitoring 52 people who had been in contact with her.
Nigerian Health Minister Muhammad Pate said the woman, the country’s first case in the current outbreak, left the capital, Abuja, early Monday with his approval. Her condition had improved significantly, and she was stable, conscious and able to communicate, he said.
“This does not mean she is not still infectious, hence the strict protocols in place,” Pate wrote on X. Her husband, a Swiss diplomat in Nigeria, has shown no symptoms.
The World Health Organization’s regional director for Africa, Mohamed Janabi, said the evacuation was arranged because the couple are Swiss citizens and that Nigerian medical teams had stabilized the woman after treating her through the acute phase of the illness.
Switzerland will take over her care and monitor her husband, while Nigeria will continue following 52 other contacts, Janabi said.
“With the evacuation of the patient and her husband, Nigeria currently has no Ebola cases,” he said, stressing that vigilance remained critical.
Pate said containment measures remained in place and urged Nigerians to remain vigilant.
The woman tested positive after returning to Abuja from Uganda. Nigerian authorities said Friday they had yet to establish how she contracted the virus.
Switzerland’s foreign ministry told The Associated Press that she had not visited Congo and was believed to have been infected while traveling to Uganda with her husband.

item.title: Australian judge rejects prisoner’s human rights challenge to Vegemite ban
item.description:
Australian judge rejects prisoner’s human rights challenge to Vegemite ban
A prisoner has lost his challenge to an Australian state’s ban on inmates eating Vegemite after he argued in court that withholding the polarizing yeast-based spread breached his human right to “enjoy his culture as an Australian.”ByROD MCGUIRK Associated PressOctober 26, 2026, 7:12 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
MELBOURNE, Australia -- A prisoner on Monday lost his challenge to an Australian state’s ban on inmates eating Vegemite after he argued in court that withholding the polarizing yeast-based spread breached his human right to “enjoy his culture as an Australian.”
Andre McKechnie, 55, who is serving a life sentence for murder, took his battle for the salty, sticky, black-brown byproduct of brewing beer to the Supreme Court of the state of Victoria last year.
He had argued being refused Vegemite denied him his right under the Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities Act to “enjoy his culture as an Australian in the community with other persons of Australian background,” court documents showed.
Justice Claire Harris accepted prison authorities’ refusal to allow McKechnie Vegemite “limited his cultural rights” under the charter.
But she found the ban was justified in meeting authorities’ goals of removing illicit drugs and alcohol from the prison system.
“The limitation on Mr. McKechnie’s ability to enjoy Vegemite in community with other persons of Australian background is primarily that he is a prisoner,” Harris wrote in her 47-page judgment.
Prison officials testified at a trial in July that Vegemite had been banned throughout the state’s 12 prisons for the past 20 years because it could potentially impair sniffer dogs’ ability to detect narcotics and could be used to brew alcohol because of its yeast content.

item.title: London’s Oxford Street bans traffic as city tries to revitalize shopping district
item.description:
London’s Oxford Street bans traffic as city tries to revitalize shopping district
London's Oxford Street is closing to cars, buses, and bicycles starting MondayByDANICA KIRKA Associated PressOctober 26, 2026, 7:05 AM
LONDON -- London’s Oxford Street will be closed to cars, buses and bicycles starting Monday as authorities seek to revive the city’s main shopping street, where the proliferation of souvenir shops and candy sellers has dimmed the allure of what was once the heart of British consumer culture.
From now on, nearly a kilometer (mile) of Oxford Street between Orchard Street and Great Portland Street will be traffic-free, with vehicles diverted onto surrounding roads. The move is the first step in a makeover of the storied shopping precinct, with plans to plant trees, install seating and add two new public squares.
Oxford Street still sees about half a million visitors a day, with shoppers bustling between retailers such as Selfridges, Zara and John Lewis.
But city officials say pedestrianizing the street will put it back into the league of top global shopping destinations like Times Square, the Champs-Élysées and La Rambla.
“This is a momentous day for London, a momentous day for Oxford Street,’’ London Mayor Sadiq Khan told the BBC. “It’s a new era.’’
While local officials began discussing the idea of pedestrianizing Oxford Street more than a decade ago, momentum began to build over the last two years when the mayor’s office created the Oxford Street Development Corporation to shepherd the project. That helped overcome opposition from local residents who complained that diverting vehicles from Oxford Street would clog their neighborhoods with traffic.
A public consultation later determined that removing traffic would attract new shops and visitors to Oxford Street, making it “an iconic destination.”

item.title: Serbia's political veteran Vucic outplayed all opponents. Then the students came
item.description:
Serbia's political veteran Vucic outplayed all opponents. Then the students came
Serbia’s populist leader Aleksandar Vucic has dominated politics in the Balkan country for 14 yearsByJOVANA GEC Associated PressOctober 26, 2026, 6:10 AM
BELGRADE, Serbia -- Serbia's populist strongman Aleksandar Vucic dominated the Balkan country's politics for 14 years. Then came the students.
The long-ruling authoritarian leader on Sunday conceded the defeat of his right-wing Serbian Progressive Party to a grassroots movement of university students who led protests for almost two years against him before unseating him in a historic change of government.
The 56-year-old political veteran easily outplayed political opponents in the past and thought he could do it again. Ahead of Sunday's ballot he pulled a maneuver in the style of his ally Russian President Vladimir Putin when he resigned the presidency to pursue a bid to become the prime minister.
Vucic then launched a fierce campaign involving favorable around-the-clock coverage on state media and attacks on opponents. He handed out cash to voters and promised higher pensions, new roads and cheaper medicines.
It didn't work. The diverse youth movement's message that rampant corruption, cronyism and organized crime under Vucic were eating away at the country resonated widely with voters.
The student protests first started in 2024 after a collapsed canopy at a renovated train station in Serbia's north killed 16 people, triggering claims that graft-fueled negligence led to poor construction work and eventually to the crash.
Defiant, Vucic on Sunday blamed his defeat on foreign interference.
“I want people to know,” he said. “This was the verification of a revolution that they carried out directly with support of different European countries and the deep American state, the one that is also against President (Donald) Trump.”

item.title: Japan's former PM Takeo Fukuda, proponent of ties with China, dies at 90
item.description:
Japan's former PM Takeo Fukuda, proponent of ties with China, dies at 90
Former Japanese Prime Minister Yasuo Fukuda, who was an active proponent of better ties with China, has diedByMARI YAMAGUCHI Associated PressOctober 26, 2026, 5:16 AM
TOKYO -- Former Japanese Prime Minister Yasuo Fukuda, who led the country for just one year and spent years afterward trying to build better ties with China, has died, officials said Monday. He was 90.
He died on Thursday, the governing Liberal Democratic Party said, without disclosing further details, including cause of his death.
Born in 1936, Fukuda grew up in a political family in Gunma, northwest of Tokyo. His father Takeo Fukuda also served as prime minister and worked to build Tokyo's ties with Beijing.
After graduating from Waseda University in Tokyo, Yasuo Fukuda worked for a Japanese oil company for more than 17 years before entering politics, first serving as his father's private secretary just before the elder Fukuda became Japan's leader in 1976.
The younger Fukuda was first elected to parliament in 1990, taking his father's former seat. He landed his first ministerial post as Chief Cabinet Secretary, or top spokesperson, for gaffe-prone then-Prime Minister Yoshiro Mori in 2000. During that time Fukuda jokingly called himself the “secretary of explanations.”
As a lawmaker, Fukuda served in a number of foreign affairs-related roles and developed a reputation as a diplomacy expert. Like his father, he placed great importance on developing friendships with Asian countries.
During his 2007-2008 prime ministership, Fukuda developed stable ties with China's Hu Jintao. Fukuda's rule lasted only one year as he struggled to manage a divided parliament in which his Liberal Democratic Party held a majority in only one of the two houses.
